notes.meaning: God has promised to dwell with his people and be their Father. Because of these wonderful promises, believers should turn away from everything that defiles the body or the inner thoughts. They are called to grow in holiness, which means living a life set apart for God, guided by deep reverence for him.

differ.view: Believers are urged to seek entire sanctification, where God's grace completely cleanses the heart from all inward sin in this life.
Believers must continually strive for complete holiness, but no one reaches sinless perfection before heaven.

notes.meaning: Paul urges the Corinthians to open their hearts fully to him and his coworkers. He reminds them of his pure motives as an apostle. He had never wronged any person, led anyone astray with false doctrine, or used ministry to cheat anyone out of money.

Paul explains that he is not trying to scold or condemn them by defending himself. He loves the Corinthians so deeply that they are bound up in his heart. He is willing to live with them or die for them as a devoted friend in Christ.

Paul feels complete freedom to speak openly to the Corinthians because he is proud of them. Even though he is facing painful trials, the good report about them fills him with comfort. His joy overflows in the middle of all his troubles.

When Paul traveled into Macedonia to find news about the church, his body found no physical rest. Opponents and persecutors fought against him on the outside. On the inside, his heart was troubled by deep worries for the believers in Corinth.

God delights to bring comfort and hope to people who are feeling crushed and discouraged. He helped Paul in his low state by sending Titus to meet him in Macedonia. Titus arrived safely with long-awaited news from Corinth.

Paul was cheered not only by seeing his friend Titus, but by hearing how well the Corinthians had treated him. Titus reported that they longed to see Paul, mourned their past errors, and were eager to support him. Hearing this turned Paul's anxiety into great joy.

Paul had sent a stern letter that caused the Corinthians real pain, and for a short time he felt bad about hurting their feelings. Now, however, he no longer regrets sending it. He sees that their grief was brief and that it produced healthy results.

Paul rejoices not because they suffered pain, but because their sorrow moved them to repent, which means changing their minds and turning away from sin. They felt the grief God wanted them to feel. Because of that, Paul's sharp warning helped them instead of causing spiritual harm.

Godly sorrow is grief that agrees with God's view of sin, producing true repentance that leads to salvation, something a believer never regrets. In contrast, worldly sorrow only regrets getting caught or suffering consequences. That selfish grief brings despair and spiritual death.

Paul highlights the clear evidence of the Corinthians' repentance. Their godly sorrow made them diligent, eager to clear their name, angry at the sin, and reverent toward God. By disciplining the offender and turning back to what was right, they showed they were innocent of endorsing evil.

Paul wrote his corrective letter with a higher goal than just focusing on the wrongdoer or the injured party. He wanted to test the whole church's loyalty to God. Through this trial, the believers saw clearly before God how much they truly cared for Paul and his guidance.

The Corinthians' healthy response brought deep comfort to Paul and his companions. On top of that comfort, Paul was overjoyed to see how happy Titus was. The church had welcomed Titus with love and completely refreshed his spirit.

Before Titus went to Corinth, Paul had praised the believers there and promised that Titus would find genuine faith among them. Paul was not put to shame, because his praise turned out to be completely true. Just as Paul had spoken God's truth to them, his boasts about them proved accurate.

Titus's love for the Corinthians grew even stronger as he remembered how quickly they obeyed God's word. They welcomed him with fear and trembling, which means with deep humility and a healthy respect for his ministry. This humble reception showed their hearts were soft toward God.

Paul wraps up this topic with gladness and courage. The report from Titus proved that the church had put away the wrong and restored good order. Paul now feels complete confidence that they will continue to follow the Lord in all matters.
